CourseName: CEN3722 - Introduction to Human Computer Interfaces

Outcomes.Text: Explain the key components of a well-defined HCI project scope.
Identify the characteristics, constraints, and capabilities of Android, iOS, Windows, and Web platforms.
Evaluate target platforms against user audience needs and project requirements.
Apply platform selection criteria to justify a specific platform choice for a design project.
Analyze appropriate design and development tools for each target platform.
Create a formal project description that documents goals, constraints, platform selection, and chosen tools.

Topics.Title: Defining Project Scope in HCI Design
Topics.Summary: This topic introduces the concept of project scoping and explains why clear boundaries and objectives are essential before beginning any HCI design project.

Elements.Title: What Is Project Scope?
Elements.BodyText: Project scope defines the boundaries of a design project, including what will and will not be addressed during the design process.
Elements.Notes: Students are coming into this module having already formed their project groups in the previous module. The scoping process is their first major collaborative task as a team.

Items.Text: Scope establishes the goals and deliverables a project aims to achieve.
Clear scope prevents feature creep and keeps the team focused throughout the design process.
A well-defined scope communicates expectations to all stakeholders.
Scope should be realistic given the team's time, skills, and resources.

Elements.Title: Identifying Project Goals
Elements.BodyText: Project goals articulate the intended outcomes of the design effort, providing direction for all subsequent design and development decisions.
Elements.Notes: Goals should be specific and measurable where possible. Encourage students to distinguish between user-facing goals (what the user should be able to do) and project goals (what the team aims to deliver).

Items.Text: Goals should describe the problem being solved and the value delivered to users.
Each goal should be specific enough to evaluate whether it has been achieved.
Goals help prioritize features and design decisions when trade-offs arise.
User-centered goals keep the design focused on real human needs rather than technical novelty.

Elements.Title: Defining Constraints
Elements.BodyText: Constraints are the limitations — such as time, budget, technology, and team expertise — that shape what is feasible within the project.
Elements.Notes: Constraints are not necessarily negative; they can sharpen focus and lead to more creative solutions. Examples include semester deadlines, group size, available tools, and the chosen platform's technical limits.

Items.Text: Time constraints define the project timeline and milestone deadlines.
Technical constraints include the capabilities and limitations of the chosen platform.
Team constraints reflect the skills and bandwidth available within the group.
Documenting constraints early prevents unrealistic expectations and scope overreach.

Elements.Title: Scoping the Target User Audience
Elements.BodyText: Understanding who will use the application is a foundational scoping decision that influences platform choice, feature prioritization, and design style.
Elements.Notes: User audience analysis connects directly to platform selection — for example, a young mobile-first audience may point toward iOS or Android, while enterprise users may favor Windows desktop applications.

Items.Text: The target audience should be described in terms of demographics, technical proficiency, and context of use.
User needs and behaviors inform which features belong inside the project scope.
The audience's access to specific devices or platforms directly impacts platform selection.
Defining the audience early aligns the entire team around a shared user vision.

Elements.Title: Writing a Formal Project Description
Elements.BodyText: The formal project description is a structured document that captures the project's goals, constraints, target audience, chosen platform, and selected tools in one authoritative reference.
Elements.Notes: This document is the primary deliverable for this module. It should be detailed enough to serve as a contract between team members about what the project is and is not.

Items.Text: A formal project description ensures all team members share a common understanding of the project.
It serves as a reference document throughout the design and development process.
The document should clearly state what is in scope and what is explicitly out of scope.
Including the rationale for key decisions, such as platform choice, strengthens the document's value.

Topics.Title: Overview of Target Application Platforms
Topics.Summary: This topic surveys the four primary platforms covered in this course — Android, iOS, Windows, and Web — and introduces additional platforms students should be aware of.

Elements.Title: The Four Primary Platforms
Elements.BodyText: This course focuses on four main application platforms: Android mobile, iOS mobile, Windows desktop, and Web-based applications, each with distinct design paradigms and audiences.
Elements.Notes: While the course focuses on these four, briefly acknowledging other platforms — such as wearables, smart TVs, voice interfaces, and AR/VR — helps students understand the broader HCI landscape.

Items.Text: Android targets a broad, global audience across a wide range of device types and price points.
iOS targets Apple device users and is associated with a more controlled, premium user experience.
Windows desktop applications serve professional, productivity-focused, and enterprise contexts.
Web applications are platform-agnostic and accessible across devices via a browser.

Elements.Title: Beyond the Four: Additional Platforms
Elements.BodyText: While this course centers on desktop, mobile, and web applications, HCI designers should be aware that interactive applications are also deployed on platforms such as wearables, voice assistants, smart TVs, and AR/VR environments.
Elements.Notes: This section provides context rather than deep instruction. Mention examples such as Apple Watch, Amazon Alexa, Android TV, and Meta Quest to illustrate the diversity of HCI contexts beyond the course's primary focus.

Items.Text: Wearable platforms such as smartwatches introduce severe screen-size and interaction constraints.
Voice interfaces require entirely different design paradigms centered on audio and conversational flow.
AR and VR platforms demand spatial design thinking beyond traditional screen-based UI.
Awareness of these platforms prepares students for evolving professional practice in HCI.

Elements.Title: Platform Categories: Mobile, Desktop, and Web
Elements.BodyText: The three broad categories of platforms — mobile, desktop, and web — each represent different user contexts, interaction models, and technical environments.
Elements.Notes: Help students understand that these categories are not mutually exclusive — for example, a Progressive Web App (PWA) can blur the line between web and mobile. Cross-platform frameworks also complicate clean categorization.

Items.Text: Mobile platforms are defined by touch interaction, portability, and on-the-go usage contexts.
Desktop platforms support complex, multi-window workflows with keyboard and mouse input.
Web platforms prioritize accessibility, cross-device reach, and browser-based deployment.
Each category has distinct human factors considerations that shape HCI design choices.

Topics.Title: Android Platform: Characteristics and Constraints
Topics.Summary: This topic examines the Android platform's key features, design conventions, user audience, and the constraints designers must account for when targeting Android.

Elements.Title: Android Platform Overview
Elements.BodyText: Android is an open-source mobile operating system developed by Google, running on a vast range of devices from numerous manufacturers worldwide.
Elements.Notes: Android's open ecosystem is both a strength and a challenge — greater market reach comes with greater fragmentation across screen sizes, hardware capabilities, and OS versions.

Items.Text: Android holds the largest global mobile market share, making it relevant for broad-reach applications.
The platform is used across smartphones, tablets, and embedded devices.
Google's Material Design system provides the standard UI guidelines for Android applications.
Android's open ecosystem results in significant device and OS version fragmentation.

Elements.Title: Android Design Conventions
Elements.BodyText: Android applications follow Material Design principles, which emphasize tactile surfaces, motion, and adaptive layouts to create consistent and intuitive user experiences.
Elements.Notes: Material Design 3 (Material You) introduced more personalization and dynamic color theming. Students should reference the official Material Design documentation when designing for Android.

Items.Text: Material Design uses elevation and shadow to communicate component hierarchy.
Navigation patterns on Android include bottom navigation bars, navigation drawers, and back gestures.
Typography, color, and spacing follow a systematic design token system in Material Design.
Adaptive layouts are essential to accommodate Android's wide range of screen sizes.

Elements.Title: Android Constraints and Considerations
Elements.BodyText: Designing for Android requires awareness of device fragmentation, varied hardware capabilities, and permission-based access to device features.
Elements.Notes: Battery optimization restrictions and background process limitations can affect app behavior in ways that differ significantly from iOS. Students should consider how their app behaves on lower-end devices.

Items.Text: Screen size and resolution vary dramatically across Android devices, requiring responsive design.
Older Android OS versions may not support newer APIs, limiting some feature implementations.
Hardware capabilities such as camera quality and processing power differ across device tiers.
User permission models on Android require thoughtful design of onboarding and access-request flows.

Topics.Title: iOS Platform: Characteristics and Constraints
Topics.Summary: This topic examines the iOS platform's design system, user audience characteristics, and the constraints inherent in Apple's more controlled ecosystem.

Elements.Title: iOS Platform Overview
Elements.BodyText: iOS is Apple's mobile operating system, powering iPhone and iPad devices, and is known for its consistency, performance, and tightly controlled hardware-software integration.
Elements.Notes: Unlike Android, iOS runs on a limited, well-defined set of devices, which reduces fragmentation and simplifies testing. This consistency is a key advantage for HCI designers.

Items.Text: iOS targets a premium device segment with a relatively affluent and tech-engaged user base.
Apple's Human Interface Guidelines (HIG) define the standards for iOS app design.
The controlled hardware ecosystem means iOS apps can be tested on a smaller set of device configurations.
iOS users tend to have high expectations for polish and performance based on Apple's brand standards.

Elements.Title: iOS Design Conventions
Elements.BodyText: iOS applications follow Apple's Human Interface Guidelines, emphasizing clarity, deference to content, and depth through layering and translucency.
Elements.Notes: Key iOS design patterns include tab bars for primary navigation, modal sheets, and swipe gestures. Students should study the HIG closely, as deviating from it can lead to App Store rejection or poor user reception.

Items.Text: Clarity means UI elements should communicate function immediately without ambiguity.
Tab bars are the primary navigation pattern for top-level sections in iOS apps.
Gesture-based navigation, including swipe-to-go-back, is a core interaction pattern.
iOS typography uses San Francisco as the system font with Dynamic Type for accessibility.

Elements.Title: iOS Constraints and Considerations
Elements.BodyText: iOS development and distribution are tightly controlled by Apple, which introduces both quality assurances and constraints for designers and developers.
Elements.Notes: App Store review guidelines significantly affect what features are permissible. Privacy is a prominent constraint — iOS requires explicit user permission for location, camera, microphone, and contact access, and these prompts must be carefully designed.

Items.Text: App Store submission requires compliance with Apple's review guidelines, which can limit certain features.
Privacy permissions must be explicitly requested and clearly justified to users.
iOS apps must support multiple device sizes, including iPhone SE through iPhone Pro Max and various iPad models.
Support for older iOS versions is a design and technical constraint that must be explicitly scoped.

Topics.Title: Windows Platform: Characteristics and Constraints
Topics.Summary: This topic covers the Windows desktop platform, its design system, typical use cases, and the unique constraints of designing for mouse, keyboard, and large-screen environments.

Elements.Title: Windows Platform Overview
Elements.BodyText: Windows is the dominant desktop operating system for personal and enterprise computing, supporting complex, feature-rich applications designed for productivity and professional use.
Elements.Notes: Windows applications are often used in workplace settings with multiple monitors, external peripherals, and long session durations — all of which are relevant HCI considerations.

Items.Text: Windows has the largest installed base of desktop operating systems globally.
The platform is especially prevalent in enterprise, education, and professional creative contexts.
Microsoft's Fluent Design System provides the current UI guidelines for Windows applications.
Windows supports both traditional Win32 applications and modern Universal Windows Platform (UWP) or WinUI apps.

Elements.Title: Windows Design Conventions
Elements.BodyText: Windows applications follow Microsoft's Fluent Design System, which emphasizes light, depth, motion, material, and scale to create coherent and accessible desktop experiences.
Elements.Notes: Students should be aware that Windows apps may need to support both touch (on Surface devices) and traditional mouse/keyboard input, requiring adaptive interaction design.

Items.Text: Fluent Design uses acrylic transparency, reveal highlights, and connected animations to add depth.
Ribbon toolbars, menu bars, and context menus are common navigation and command patterns.
Keyboard shortcuts and accessibility features are first-class concerns in Windows application design.
Windows apps must account for window resizing, multi-window usage, and varying display densities.

Elements.Title: Windows Constraints and Considerations
Elements.BodyText: Designing for Windows involves accounting for a wide range of hardware configurations, OS versions still in use, and the expectations of productivity-focused users.
Elements.Notes: Enterprise environments often run older OS versions and have strict IT policies that limit what applications can do. If the target audience includes enterprise users, this must be scoped explicitly.

Items.Text: Hardware variation includes differences in screen resolution, DPI scaling, and input devices.
Enterprise users may be locked to specific Windows versions, constraining the use of newer APIs.
Productivity users expect high information density, keyboard control, and multi-tasking support.
Accessibility standards such as WCAG and Microsoft's own guidelines must be integrated from the start.

Topics.Title: Web Platform: Characteristics and Constraints
Topics.Summary: This topic explores the web as an application platform, covering its cross-device reach, design considerations, browser constraints, and suitability for different project types.

Elements.Title: Web Platform Overview
Elements.BodyText: Web applications run in browsers and are accessible across virtually all devices and operating systems without requiring installation, making the web the most universally accessible platform.
Elements.Notes: Web applications range from simple informational sites to complex single-page applications (SPAs) that rival native apps in functionality. The distinction between a website and a web app is relevant for scoping purposes.

Items.Text: Web apps are accessed via URLs and run in browsers such as Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge.
The web platform requires no installation, lowering the barrier to user adoption significantly.
Responsive design is essential to ensure usability across desktop, tablet, and mobile browsers.
Web apps can be made available offline and installable via Progressive Web App (PWA) technology.

Elements.Title: Web Design Conventions
Elements.BodyText: Web application design is guided by established usability conventions, WCAG accessibility standards, and responsive design principles rather than a single platform's design system.
Elements.Notes: Unlike native platforms, the web does not have one canonical design system. Designers may use frameworks such as Material Design for Web, Apple Human Interface principles adapted for web, or custom design systems. Accessibility compliance (WCAG 2.1 AA) is a baseline expectation.

Items.Text: Navigation patterns on the web include top navigation bars, hamburger menus, and sidebar panels.
Typography, color contrast, and layout must meet WCAG accessibility standards.
Responsive breakpoints ensure the layout adapts appropriately from mobile to widescreen displays.
Familiar web conventions, such as underlined links and breadcrumb trails, should not be violated without clear reason.

Elements.Title: Web Platform Constraints and Considerations
Elements.BodyText: Web applications are constrained by browser compatibility, network dependency, security sandboxing, and the limitations of web APIs compared to native platform APIs.
Elements.Notes: Browser inconsistencies, while reduced by modern standards, still require cross-browser testing. Students should also consider what happens to their app in low-connectivity scenarios.

Items.Text: Browser support must be explicitly scoped — older browsers may not support modern CSS or JavaScript APIs.
Web apps have limited access to native device hardware compared to native mobile or desktop apps.
Network latency and offline scenarios must be planned for in the design and architecture.
Security constraints in the browser sandbox restrict certain interactions with the file system and OS.

Topics.Title: Platform Selection: Criteria and Decision-Making
Topics.Summary: This topic provides a framework for evaluating and selecting the most appropriate platform for a given HCI project, based on audience, goals, and constraints.

Elements.Title: User Audience as a Primary Driver
Elements.BodyText: The most important factor in platform selection is matching the platform to where the target users actually are and how they prefer to interact with technology.
Elements.Notes: Encourage students to ground their platform choice in evidence about their target audience rather than personal preference. A student who prefers iOS should still choose Android if the target users are primarily on Android.

Items.Text: Identify what devices the target users primarily own and use in their daily lives.
Consider the context of use — whether the app will be used on the go, at a desk, or in both contexts.
User technical proficiency may favor platforms with more familiar interaction patterns.
Accessibility needs of the target audience may make certain platforms more suitable than others.

Elements.Title: Platform Capability Alignment
Elements.BodyText: The project's required features must align with what the chosen platform can support, including hardware access, performance requirements, and available APIs.
Elements.Notes: A project requiring persistent background location tracking will be better served by a native mobile app than a web app. Students should map each key feature to platform capabilities early in the scoping process.

Items.Text: Identify the hardware features the application requires, such as camera, GPS, or sensors.
Match performance-intensive features to platforms with appropriate native support.
Evaluate whether web APIs are sufficient or whether native platform APIs are necessary.
Consider offline functionality requirements and how each platform handles them.

Elements.Title: Team Skills and Tool Availability
Elements.BodyText: The practical skills of the project team and the availability of appropriate tools should factor into the platform decision, particularly within an academic project context.
Elements.Notes: In a course setting, it is reasonable to factor in what tools and technologies students already know or can realistically learn within the semester. This is a legitimate scoping constraint.

Items.Text: Assess the team's existing programming and design skills relevant to each platform.
Consider the learning curve associated with platform-specific tools and frameworks.
Tool availability, including licenses, hardware requirements, and operating system compatibility, may limit options.
Choosing a platform the team can realistically deliver on is itself a valid design decision.

Elements.Title: Documenting and Justifying the Platform Choice
Elements.BodyText: The platform selection decision must be explicitly documented in the formal project description, including the rationale based on audience, capability, and team constraints.
Elements.Notes: A well-justified platform choice demonstrates design thinking and sets up all subsequent decisions. Students should be able to articulate why their chosen platform is the best fit, not just why they like it.

Items.Text: State the chosen platform clearly and unambiguously in the project description.
Provide a rationale that references user audience analysis, feature requirements, and team constraints.
Acknowledge any trade-offs or limitations accepted as a result of the platform choice.
The documented rationale should be persuasive to a stakeholder unfamiliar with the project.

Topics.Title: Design and Development Tools by Platform
Topics.Summary: This topic surveys the appropriate design, prototyping, and development tools available for each platform, helping students select a suitable toolchain for their project.

Elements.Title: Design and Prototyping Tools
Elements.BodyText: Regardless of platform, HCI projects typically begin with wireframing and prototyping tools that allow designers to explore and test ideas before committing to development.
Elements.Notes: Figma is widely used in the industry and is recommended for this course due to its collaboration features. Other tools such as Adobe XD and Sketch are also commonly used. Students should use the tool their team is most comfortable with, provided it supports the target platform's design conventions.

Items.Text: Figma supports collaborative design, prototyping, and handoff for all four primary platforms.
Platform-specific UI kits are available in Figma for Material Design, iOS HIG, and Fluent Design.
Wireframing tools such as Balsamiq are useful for low-fidelity ideation before high-fidelity design.
Prototyping tools should support the interaction patterns native to the chosen platform.

Elements.Title: Android Development Tools
Elements.BodyText: Android application development is primarily done using Android Studio, Google's official IDE, with Kotlin as the recommended programming language.
Elements.Notes: For HCI-focused projects, students do not necessarily need to build fully functional apps — high-fidelity Figma prototypes may be sufficient. However, awareness of development tools is important for realistic scoping.

Items.Text: Android Studio provides layout editors, emulators, and debugging tools for Android development.
Kotlin is the modern, preferred language for Android development over the legacy Java approach.
Jetpack Compose is Google's modern toolkit for building native Android UI with a declarative approach.
The Android Emulator allows testing across various virtual device configurations without physical hardware.

Elements.Title: iOS Development Tools
Elements.BodyText: iOS applications are developed using Xcode, Apple's IDE, with Swift as the primary programming language, both of which require a macOS computer.
Elements.Notes: The macOS requirement is a significant hardware constraint for teams without Apple computers. If team members do not have Macs, iOS development may be impractical, making this a real scoping constraint to acknowledge.

Items.Text: Xcode is the required IDE for iOS development and is only available on macOS.
Swift is Apple's modern, safe, and expressive programming language for iOS development.
SwiftUI enables declarative UI construction and is the current preferred framework for new iOS projects.
The iOS Simulator in Xcode enables testing on virtual iPhone and iPad models.

Elements.Title: Windows Development Tools
Elements.BodyText: Windows applications are developed primarily using Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code, with languages and frameworks such as C#, WinUI 3, and .NET being the standard choices.
Elements.Notes: Windows development tools are available for free via Visual Studio Community edition. Students targeting Windows should also be aware of the Windows App SDK and how it differs from the older Universal Windows Platform approach.

Items.Text: Visual Studio is the primary IDE for Windows application development with rich UI design support.
C# with WinUI 3 is the recommended modern stack for building native Windows applications.
The Windows App SDK provides a unified set of APIs for building modern Windows desktop apps.
XAML is used to define the UI layout and structure in WinUI-based Windows applications.

Elements.Title: Web Development Tools
Elements.BodyText: Web application development uses browser-based and cross-platform tools, with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript forming the foundational technology stack.
Elements.Notes: Visual Studio Code is the dominant code editor for web development and is free and cross-platform. Students may use frameworks such as React, Vue, or Angular depending on their experience, but complexity should be scoped appropriately for the project timeline.

Items.Text: Visual Studio Code is a widely used, free, cross-platform editor suitable for web development.
HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are the foundational technologies for all web applications.
Frameworks such as React, Vue, and Angular can accelerate development but add learning complexity.
Browser developer tools in Chrome and Firefox are essential for debugging and performance testing.

Elements.Title: Cross-Platform Tools and Frameworks
Elements.BodyText: Cross-platform frameworks allow a single codebase to target multiple platforms, which can be advantageous for teams with limited resources but introduces trade-offs in native experience quality.
Elements.Notes: Examples include Flutter (Android and iOS from one codebase), React Native (mobile), and Electron (desktop from web technologies). Students choosing cross-platform tools should still scope their project to a primary platform for HCI evaluation purposes.

Items.Text: Flutter allows development of Android and iOS apps from a single Dart codebase.
React Native enables mobile app development using JavaScript and React.
Electron wraps web applications into desktop apps for Windows, macOS, and Linux.
Cross-platform tools may sacrifice platform-specific UI conventions, which is an HCI trade-off to evaluate.
